summary: Sam posts pre-departure reflections as fundraising pitch drafts are underway; the trip is described as about 4000 miles from San Francisco to Washington, D.C.
planning_notes: 2014 route was stated as about 4000 miles, San Francisco to Washington, D.C.
Donations were solicited through a Google Form linked from the blog; Facebook and Twitter used for updates

summary: Cali writes about her philosophy of self-driven learning, drawing on her ESP immunology teaching, and says Spokes will help students find their own answers.
planning_notes: Teaching approach that worked for Cali: let students lead questions and find answers themselves instead of lecturing; she tells students she may not know the answer

summary: Jamin reflects on his fear of stepping outside his comfort zone before the trip and hopes the ride will build character and inspire students to try new things.
Evan reports the whole team has assembled at a host family's backyard in Menlo Park, CA, pitching tents and doing laundry, bike shop stop, packing the car and a short ride before departure.
slept_at: Caroline Wang and family's backyard, Menlo Park, CA (family host; 2014-06-15 post says San Francisco)
contacts: Caroline Wang, Mike and Christopher, Menlo Park CA (hosted team in backyard for pre-trip prep)
planning_notes: Pre-departure base: a host family's backyard in the Bay Area gave room for tents, sorting gear and packing the van before the start
Bike shop in the Bay Area used for last-minute supplies before leaving

summary: Cali, driving the van, recaps the hot first days around Sacramento (pavement 103-108 F) and the start of hills; the riders left at 5:30 am while she drove.
slept_at: Lake Soleno campsite (campground; location not stated)
planning_notes: Central California heat: pavement hit 103-108 F in the afternoon; riders napped by the American River in the hottest hours, and leaving before dawn was the answer
American River Trail bike path (Sacramento area) was pleasant and busy with serious cyclists
Lake Soleno campsite has peacocks that are very loud all night; the entrance has a cooling sprinkler
Ibuprofen was needed for IT band pain in the first days, so start hydrating and getting up earlier

summary: Answers a reader question: four team members with licenses alternate driving the van so everyone gets a rest day.
planning_notes: Van driving rota: four licensed team members alternate driving days; a driving day doubles as a rest day for the rider, so the whole team does not need to rest at once

summary: Riders climb to Carson Pass in the Sierra Nevada, descend a steep grade toward Woodfords CA, and ride into Carson City NV, where three nights and a first library workshop are planned.
slept_at: Carson City, NV (3 nights planned; lodging not named)
learning_festival: First teaching workshop planned at Carson City Public Library, the following Monday
contacts: Kevin, volunteer park ranger at Carson Pass, avid cyclist who may ride with the team in Colorado
planning_notes: Carson Pass (Sierra Nevada, about 8600 ft) is a long grinding climb; the far side has a roughly 4 mile, 8% grade descent
Daily routine that worked: wake 4-4:30 am, ride out of camp 5:15 am, reach next campsite by noon, then lunch, nap, dinner, bed about 8:30
Early starts in the Sierra are freezing at 4:30 am; warm layers are needed even while riding
2014 sponsors credited: IAC, Texas Instruments, It's About Time, Harvard SEAS and MIT

summary: Rest day in Carson City NV at an RV campground; the team plans its first workshop, learns about Nevada history at Bike Habitat, and crosses the California-Nevada border.
slept_at: RV campground, Carson City, NV (name not stated)
contacts: Dennis and Jeremiah, Bike Habitat, Carson City NV (bike shop; shared local history)
Texas Instruments company blog (ran a post about the team)
planning_notes: RV campground in Carson City NV is a workable rest-day base for bike riders: showers, Wi-Fi and a hot tub
Bike Habitat in Carson City NV is a local bike shop the team visited on its rest day
Sierra climbs to the pass took about three days; freezing mornings need all the clothes you packed
Genoa NV is Nevada's oldest settlement and has the state's oldest bar

summary: Emma reports from Fallon NV that the team finished its first teaching stop at the Carson City library and is handling logistics and communications; the post is truncated.
learning_festival: Carson City, NV public library, first teaching stop, described as a great first experience
contacts: Carson City, NV public library (first LF host)

summary: Emma recounts riding into Austin NV and camping in the town park, meeting retired engineers who maintain Pony Express trail signs, and an evening at Middlegate NV, plus a reflection on purpose.
slept_at: Local town park campsite, Austin NV (a couple of nights before this post); Prospector Hotel and Casino (current stop; location not stated)
contacts: Dick and Don, Emigrant Trails Inc (retired engineers who put up historic trail signs), met in Austin NV park
Paul Smith, local guitarist, Middlegate NV
Middlegate NV bar and restaurant (only food and drink for about 50 miles on Highway 50)
planning_notes: Highway 50 in Nevada is very remote: Middlegate NV (population 17) is the only bar and restaurant for about 50 miles in either direction

Middlegate runs entirely on generators and spends several thousand dollars a month on diesel, replacing generators several times a year; they are struggling to stay open, so a donation or sponsor contact is a possible give-back
Austin NV: camping in the local park worked; long straight stretches of road are lonely on the bike

summary: Emma writes from Cedar City UT about road debris seen in Nevada and Utah, a rest-day climb of Mt. Wheeler in Great Basin National Park, and a swim in a cold lake.
planning_notes: Road shoulders between Nevada and Utah are littered with tire strips, beer cans, shotgun shells and shot-up road signs; watch for debris
Great Basin National Park (NV): Mt. Wheeler trail is 3.1 miles from about 10,000 ft, gaining about 3000 ft; lakes below the summit are freezing for a swim

summary: Cali writes from Escalante UT about climbing Cedar Breaks and riding through Red Canyon, Bryce Canyon and Grand Staircase, plus lessons from a Cedar City girl scout workshop that became a bicycle and tinkering session.
learning_festival: Cedar City UT park, late afternoon: two dozen girl scouts ages 5-10 in three pair-led workshops; Maddie and Cali ran a bicycle and tinkering station (sprockets, hubs, tires, flats, magnets, electricity) and let kids take apart a blender motor
contacts: Girl Scout group, Cedar City UT (about two dozen girls ages 5-10)
planning_notes: Cedar Breaks National Monument (UT): a climb of 20-plus miles up to 10,350 ft; the overlook entry fee was $4
Bike tinkering station works well for kids: let them take apart a blender motor, and prep a bike-powered blender as backup
Kids ages 5-10 are open and take a teacher at their word; parents, especially at the girl scout stop, valued seeing girls do engineering hands-on
Asking kids what sticks to magnets gave a non-textbook answer; use open questions rather than just correcting

summary: Emma reflects on childhood biking and on a 20-mile, roughly 4000 ft climb in painful heat, describing the satisfaction of arriving at each day's campsite after nine-hour rides.
planning_notes: Western highways: RVs pass very close on the shoulder and keep riders on edge; ride defensively
Long climbs in dry western heat: sunblock melts and dries out skin; plan water and shade on 9-hour riding days

summary: Emma reports from Boulder CO after riding the Rockies, including the first century, Loveland Pass at 11,990 ft, a July 3 mountain hailstorm, a Telluride stay with the Pinhead Institute, and a bike-carried solar model in the 4th of July parade.
slept_at: Boulder, CO (hosts not named in post)
learning_festival: No workshops in Telluride; the team built a bicycle-carried solar system model and rode with the Pinhead Institute in the Telluride 4th of July parade
contacts: Sarah, Executive Director of the Pinhead Institute of Telluride CO (STEM center; team stayed with her)
planning_notes: Pinhead Institute (Telluride CO) runs week-long summer STEM camps with local engineers and scientists and has arranged tech internships for high schoolers; a good partner for LF-style programming
Telluride CO: a bike-carried solar model fit in the 4th of July parade and was a good local-visibility move
Colorado mountains: afternoon thunderstorms with hail on July 3; riders caught out were frozen, so pack warm layers
Loveland Pass (11,990 ft) was the highest point of the trip so far; Monarch Pass crossed the Continental Divide
The Golden CO to Boulder CO final 30 miles were the navigation test of the day

summary: Sam reports a 120-mile day along US-34 from Brush CO to St. Francis KS, crossing a corner of Nebraska and passing a train at the border; a Loveland CO library stop came before the Amelia Earhart festival in Atchison KS.
learning_festival: Loveland, CO library stop; upcoming Amelia Earhart Festival booth in Atchison, KS
planning_notes: US-34 in northeast Colorado is a long, monotonous road past cattle farms and livestock trucks
Routing through the southwest corner of Nebraska cost no extra distance from the north-Colorado route; about 10 miles in Nebraska
Northwest Kansas has about 400 miles of mostly straight east-west riding

summary: Emma reports halfway through northern Kansas at Seneca KS, with daily cornfield riding and friendly drivers who waved often.
planning_notes: Northern Kansas drivers were friendlier, waved more and sped less than elsewhere on the route

summary: Jamin reports from St. Louis at the halfway point: a booth at the Amelia Earhart Festival in Atchison KS, Missouri's steep hills, the Katy Trail's crushed limestone surface, and a rest day ahead.
learning_festival: Booth in the kids' section at the Amelia Earhart Festival, Atchison KS (met a snake too)
contacts: Turner, past Spokes team founder, joined as a guest rider on the Katy Trail
planning_notes: Katy Trail (MO) is crushed limestone; road-bike tires held up and the team had only one flat
Missouri: take a state route rather than the scenic county road, which had steep blind hills
Kansas was crossed in 4 days in order to reach the Atchison festival

summary: Emma describes a Lego workshop on lean manufacturing and design-for-assembly run at a Loveland CO library and the Atchison KS festival, where kids designed robots and reassembled a bicycle hub.
learning_festival: Loveland CO library and Amelia Earhart Festival (Atchison KS): open-table format, each rider had a table; Lego design-for-manufacturing workshop, then a bike wheel hub teardown and reassembly
planning_notes: Lego DFA workshop: let kids design their own robot first, then iterate on it; this worked better than dictating a design
Legos drew kids of all ages and kids whose first language is not English, even with competing booths at the Atchison festival
Bike hub teardown then reassembly: 8-year-olds handled bearings and grease without trouble; borrow a hub from the bike tinkering table

summary: Emma writes from Carbondale IL after three day-long workshops in six days (homeschool group in Milstadt IL, maker space in Farmington MO, science center in Carbondale IL) and argues teamwork helps kids learn STEM.
learning_festival: Three day-long workshops in six days: homeschool group in Milstadt IL, maker space in Farmington MO, science center in Carbondale IL; Lego manufacturing, Launchpad lightshow, bike tinkering
planning_notes: Team-based workshop format: kids in teams built faster and tried bolder designs than kids working alone, and the team set a 32-iteration record in under 2 minutes
Older kids helping younger kids in tinkering worked well; the team noticed peer teaching across ages

summary: Cali reflects on the impact of teaching and talking with parents, and on a Week of Code session at Awesome, Inc., a start-up incubator, from Portsmouth, Ohio.
learning_festival: Week of Code at Awesome, Inc. (start-up incubator and co-working space)
contacts: Awesome, Inc. (start-up incubator and co-working space; location not stated)
planning_notes: Talking with parents about one's own path mattered almost as much as teaching the kids; a visible 'ordinary' college student is a useful role model
